title: Pauri 1, meaning: the wall of falsehood
hook: thinking a hundred thousand times cannot reach Him; the wall of falsehood falls by walking in His order (Japji 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of the first pauri. Your line was sochai soch. Did you catch your mind pacing, and name the loop? Day one hundred sixty-four.

Most of us have a few tricks for getting closer to what matters. Think harder: one more lap around the problem. Go quiet: a retreat, the phone in a drawer. Get more: the next purchase, the next raise will settle it. Get cleverer: one more book, one more podcast. Guru Nanak's first pauri takes tricks like these one at a time and gently closes each door. Then it opens a different one.
screen: `THINK HARDER. GO QUIET.` → `GET MORE. GET CLEVERER.` → `FOUR DOORS, GENTLY CLOSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. By thinking, He can't be reached, though you think a hundred thousand times. By keeping silent, you don't become silent inside, though you sit absorbed without end. The hunger of the hungry isn't satisfied, even by heaping up the goods of all the worlds. You may have a hundred thousand clevernesses, and not one of them goes with you. Four tricks: thought, silence, having, cleverness. None of them is wicked. They just can't get you there. Some readers hear the first line as ritual cleansing rather than thinking: washing a hundred thousand times won't make the mind clean. Either way, the effort alone falls short. Then comes the question. Kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai, kiv koorhai tutai paal? How do we become true? How is the wall of falsehood torn down? Paal is a wall, a bank, the kind that walls off a field. Koorh is the false, the fake. So there's a wall made of falsehood standing between us and the true. And the answer: hukam rajaaee chalnaa, Naanak likhiaa naal. Walk in the hukam of the One whose will it is, written, says Nanak, along with us. Hukam is a word you'll hear all through Sikh life. It means an order, a command, the way a ruler's word goes out. But in Japji it's bigger: the order of things, the will running through everything, the way the world actually is. You met a daily piece of it in camp three, the hukamnama. The wall doesn't come down by out-thinking it. It comes down by walking in step.
screen: `FOUR DOORS THAT DON'T OPEN.` · `KOORH — THE WALL OF FALSEHOOD.` · `HUKAM — THE ORDER, THE WILL.` · `WALK IN STEP WITH IT.` · then, large: `HUKAM.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you've been turning over: a decision, a conversation, a worry. Hold it for one breath. Now, instead of thinking about it again, set it down in front of you, like a bag you've carried too far. Feel your feet on the floor. Feel the breath going in and out on its own, without your help. That breath is already walking in the order, without a single thought. Stay with it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru carry the bag for a while. The bell holds the time.
Hukam. The order, the will running through everything. Japji's first pauri says the wall of falsehood falls by walking in it.
Your line: walk in the order. When you catch yourself overthinking today, stand up and take ten slow steps instead of one more lap. Day one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the first pauri every morning in Japji; hukam is central to Sikh teaching, and the daily hukamnama read from the Guru Granth Sahib is received as the order for that day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a command, like a boss gives.
what it means: the order of things, the will running through everything; the wall of falsehood falls by walking in it.
what a scholar hears: hukam and razaa come into Punjabi from Arabic through Persian; Guru Nanak's vocabulary draws on both Indian and Persian words.
